newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Kuwait sets record naphtha price amid Asian demand.
newsitem.headline: Kuwait sets record naphtha price amid Asian demand.

text.p: Kuwait has set a record price for its latest sales of naphtha to petrochemical companies in Asia, reflecting increasing demand from region, industry sources said on Friday.

State-owned Kuwait Petroleum Corp (KPC) has set naphtha term sales contracts with Asian buyers at $13.50 per tonne over spot Mideast quotes for 2.7 million tonnes lifting March 1997-February 1998, a company source said.
"It is a very good premium because demand for this region is expanding," said a Japanese trader.
Naphtha demand in the Asia-Pacific region will grow to 488,000 barrels-per-day (bpd) this year from 417,000-bpd in 1994, according to the Honolulu-based East-West Center.
This year, Asia naphtha demand is expected to grow by 2.3 million tonnes (60,000-bpd), while supplies are expected to rise by 1.8 million to 2.3 million tonnes, a Japanese refiner said.
Demand and spot prices have been boosted by several new petrochemical plants coming onstream in India, Singapore and Thailand this year.
Meanwhile, the new plants are expected to push down the prices of petrochemicals, including ethylene, in the next two to three years and eat into profits, industry sources said.
"But it (the KPC premium) is also very expensive," said one trader. "Margins are getting worse because the naphtha feed (price) is high but there is too much competition in the ethylene market."
Diminishing profits prompted Japan's largest petrochemical company, Mitsubishi Chemical Corp to cut its 1.45 million tonne-per-year ethylene production by 10 percent in January.

Earlier this month, Idemitsu Petrochemical Co Ltd followed suit with cuts of 12 percent at its 365,000 tonne-per-year Chiba plant, while South Korea's largest refiner Yukong Ltd closed down two reformers as due to the squeeze on profits.
But KPC sources said they were sympathetic towards the poor state of the petrochemical market.
"It is the highest premium since at least the liberation of Kuwait," the KPC source told Reuters.

"But we haven't really taken advantage ot the upward trend of the naphtha market. When evaluating the premium, we have taken the end-users' into consideration... the petrochemical situation has not really been in a good situation," he said.

KPC renewed the contracts with 10 buyers from Japan for 1.5 million tonnes and four South Korea buyers for 900,000 tonnes while signing a new contract with India's Reliance Industries for 300,000 tonnes.
Reliance is one of the new plants in the region, which started up a 700,000 tonne-per-year in December and due to operate at full capacity by March.

KPC's new premium is nearly double set in its two rounds of term contracts in 1996 - $7.90 for 2.6-2.7 million tonnes lifting August 1996-September 1997 and $6.50 for March 1996-February 1997 supplies.

Naphtha term prices were already on the rise with Asian buyers settling in October last year on a higher premium for Saudi Aramco's A-180 naphtha supplies in the first half of this year of $6.50, up by $2.50 to $3.10.

Bahrain National Oil Co (BANOCO) set a premium of $11.00-$11.50 for its one-year term sales for about one million tonnes of naphtha, while Caltex Bahrain settled on even a higher premium of around $16.00 at the begining of this year but for a smaller volume of 150,000 tonnes lifting in the second half of the year, traders said.
The last round of term negotiations for the year -- KPC's second round of supplies lifting August 1997-September 1998 -- is due sometime in June to July in London.
Asian traders said they expected prices to remain stable at current levels.
"It has reached its peak already," a Japanese trader said.
--Singapore Newsroom (+65-870-3086)
